learningJourney.title: What is Bitmask Dynamic Programming
learningJourney.explanation:
When a problem's optimal substructure depends only on *which* subset $S$ of $n$ items has been used (and optionally the last item), all permutations of $S$ collapse into a single DP state. **Bitmask DP** encodes $S \subseteq \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ as an $n$-bit integer `mask` where bit $i$ is `1` iff item $i \in S$.

Setting one unvisited bit (`mask | (1 << j)`) strictly increases the integer value of `mask`, giving a built-in topological DAG order over `0 .. (1 << n) - 1` and reducing $n!$ permutations to $O(n 2^n)$ or $O(n^2 2^n)$.

sectionDiagram.title: Held-Karp TSP State Compression (0001 -> 0011 -> 0111 -> 1111)
sectionDiagram.summary: Because setting a bit strictly increases mask, iterating mask from 0 to (1<<n)-1 processes states in valid topological order.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Bitmask Compression (and complexity/memory traps)
learningJourney.explanation:
At $n = 18$, $18! \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15}$ is impossible, whereas $18^2 \cdot 2^{18} \approx 8.5 \times 10^7$ runs in under a second.

Watch three classic pitfalls:
1. **Accidental $O(4^n)$ Submask Loop**: Iterating `0..2^n-1` inside `0..2^n-1` takes $1.07 \times 10^9$ ops at $n=15$, whereas `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` takes $O(3^n) \approx 1.4 \times 10^7$.
2. **Redundant Dimension in Assignment**: When assigning item `i` to worker `k`, you only need `dp[mask]` (not `dp[i][mask]`) because `popcount(mask)` uniquely determines `i`!
3. **OOM on 2D `long` Tables**: `long[1 << 20][20]` uses 160 MB.

When a problem's optimal substructure depends only on *which* subset $S$ of $n$ items has been used (and optionally the last item), all permutations of $S$ collapse into a single DP state. **Bitmask DP** encodes $S \subseteq \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ as an $n$-bit integer `mask` where bit $i$ is `1` iff item $i \in S$.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Bitmask Compression (and complexity/memory traps)
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Bitmask Compression under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
At $n = 18$, $18! \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15}$ is impossible, whereas $18^2 \cdot 2^{18} \approx 8.5 \times 10^7$ runs in under a second.

Watch three classic pitfalls:
1. **Accidental $O(4^n)$ Submask Loop**: Iterating `0..2^n-1` inside `0..2^n-1` takes $1.07 \times 10^9$ ops at $n=15$, whereas `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` takes $O(3^n) \approx 1.4 \times 10^7$.
2. **Redundant Dimension in Assignment**: When assigning item `i` to worker `k`, you only need `dp[mask]` (not `dp[i][mask]`) because `popcount(mask)` uniquely determines `i`!
3. **OOM on 2D `long` Tables**: `long[1 << 20][20]` uses 160 MB.

concepts.name: Bloom Filters, Counting Bloom & Cuckoo Filters
concepts.tagline: Space-optimal probabilistic set membership: zero false negatives, tunable false positives, and deletion trade-offs via Cuckoo fingerprinting.
concepts.purpose: Choose and size Bloom, Counting Bloom, and Cuckoo filters for SSTable point lookups, cache-penetration shields, and dynamic blocklists.

spark.summary: Bloom filters answer set membership in O(k) bit probes using ~10 bits per key at a 1% false-positive rate with zero false negatives, while Cuckoo filters store compact fingerprints in 2-choice hash buckets to support safe item deletion and better CPU cache locality.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never delete from a standard Bloom filter (it clears bits shared by other keys); use a Cuckoo filter when items must be removed dynamically or when low false-positive rates (<3%) need tighter memory.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A **Bloom Filter** hashes key `x` with `k` functions into a bit array (`0` bit = definitely absent; all `1`s = probably present with false-positive rate `p`). Standard Bloom filters cannot delete items. **Cuckoo Filters** store short `f`-bit fingerprints in two candidate buckets (`b1 = h1(x)`, `b2 = b1 XOR h(fp)`), supporting deletion and eviction swaps.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Contrasts a `Bloom Filter (No Delete)` (`x` -> `h1, h2, h3` -> bit array `[0|1|0|1|1|0|1]`) against a `Cuckoo Filter (Supports Delete)` (`2-choice hash buckets` `b1, b2` holding `[fp]` fingerprints with `Evict & Kick Swap`).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** At `1%` false-positive rate, a Bloom filter uses ~9.6 bits/key, whereas a Counting Bloom filter uses 4x memory (`4-bit` counters) and risks counter overflow. Cuckoo filters use ~12.6 bits/key (or less at `<3%` FP) with 2 cache-line reads instead of `k` random probes.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Never exceed a Cuckoo filter's ~95% load factor (eviction loops fail inserts) and never delete a non-existent key from a Cuckoo filter if duplicate inserts are possible.

learningJourney.title: How Bloom Filters & Cuckoo Filters Work
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand bitset probing in Bloom filters vs. XOR-linked fingerprint buckets in Cuckoo filters.
learningJourney.explanation:
A **Bloom Filter** allocates `m` bits and `k` independent hash functions. Inserting `x` sets bits `h_1(x)...h_k(x)` to `1`. Querying `x` returns **definitely absent** if any bit is `0`, or **probably present** if all `k` bits are `1` (false-positive rate `p`). Optimal sizing uses `m = -(n * ln(p)) / (ln(2)^2)` bits (~9.6 bits/key for `p = 1%`) and `k = (m/n) * ln(2)` (~7 probes).

A **Cuckoo Filter** replaces the bitset with buckets of `b = 4` fingerprint slots. Each key `x` yields an `f`-bit fingerprint `fp` and two candidate buckets: `b1 = hash(x)` and `b2 = b1 XOR hash(fp)`. Notice `b1` can be computed from `b2` using only `fp` (`b1 = b2 XOR hash(fp)`), allowing items to be **relocated** when a bucket fills and **deleted** by removing one matching `fp`.

cards.label: Zero False Negatives
cards.detail: If neither b1 nor b2 holds fp, key x is guaranteed absent.

cards.label: Cache Locality
cards.detail: Checks at most 2 buckets (2 cache lines) vs. k=7..10 random bit probes.

cards.label: Safe Deletion
cards.detail: Removes 1 matching fp from b1 or b2 without affecting other keys.

sectionDiagram.summary: Caption: Cuckoo filters use partial-key cuckoo hashing (b2 = b1 XOR h(fp)) to relocate and delete items using only the stored fingerprint.

learningJourney.title: Why You Cannot Delete From a Standard Bloom Filter
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see how clearing a bit in a Bloom filter corrupts unrelated keys and creates false negatives.
learningJourney.explanation: Because multiple keys hash onto overlapping bit positions, clearing a `1` bit to `0` when deleting `key_A` can silently break `key_B`—violating the **zero false negatives** invariant. Meanwhile, **Counting Bloom Filters** replace each bit with a 4-bit counter (4x RAM overhead) and suffer counter overflow if a hot key is inserted repeatedly.

learningJourney.title: Where Bloom vs. Cuckoo Filters Fit Best
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: match immutable SSTables to Bloom filters and mutable blocklists/caches to Cuckoo filters.
learningJourney.explanation: Use **standard Bloom filters** for **immutable** datasets such as RocksDB/LevelDB SSTable blocks or daily batch snapshots. Use **Cuckoo filters** for **mutable** sets (session revocation lists, CDN one-hit-wonder admission caches, or active feature-flag memberships) where entries are frequently added and removed.

learningJourney.title: Sizing Bits-per-Key, Load Factor & Rebuild Thresholds
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: bound Cuckoo load factor below 95% and guard against insertion failure.
learningJourney.explanation: Size Bloom filters with explicit `(n, p)` budgets (`~10 bits/key` for `1%` FP, `~14.4 bits/key` for `0.1%` FP). For Cuckoo filters, cap occupancy at **90–95%** (`bucket_size = 4`) and bound eviction loops (`max_kicks = 500`); if an insert exhausts `max_kicks`, trigger an asynchronous double-capacity rebuild.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
import math

def bloom_sizing(expected_items: int, fp_rate: float) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (num_bits, num_hashes) for target expected_items and false-positive rate."""
    if expected_items <= 0 or not (0 < fp_rate < 1):
        raise ValueError("expected_items must be > 0 and 0 < fp_rate < 1")
    m = int(math.ceil(-(expected_items * math.log(fp_rate)) / (math.log(2) ** 2)))
    k = max(1, int(round((m / expected_items) * math.log(2))))
    return m, k
```

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does deleting a key by clearing its bits in a standard Bloom filter break correctness?

options.text: Other inserted keys may share those bit positions, so clearing them introduces false negatives
options.feedback: Correct: Bloom filters forbid deletion because multiple keys map to overlapping bits.

options.text: Clearing bits doubles the false-positive rate immediately
options.feedback: Incorrect: clearing bits causes false negatives, not false positives.

options.text: Bloom filters only store 1 bit total
options.feedback: Incorrect: Bloom filters use m bits across k hash probes.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does a Cuckoo filter compute a key's alternate bucket b2 during eviction without storing the original key?

options.text: Using partial-key cuckoo hashing: b2 = b1 XOR hash(fp)
options.feedback: Correct: XOR is self-inverse, so b1 and b2 can always be derived from each other using only the compact fingerprint fp.

options.text: By querying the backing PostgreSQL database on every kick
options.feedback: Incorrect: Cuckoo filters stay 100% in memory with zero DB lookups.

options.text: By scanning all buckets linearly
options.feedback: Incorrect: lookup and relocation are O(1) across exactly two candidate buckets.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if you insert into a Cuckoo filter that is >95% full?

options.text: Eviction kick chains can cycle and hit max_kicks, requiring a resize/rebuild
options.feedback: Correct: Cuckoo filters degrade sharply above ~95% occupancy and must be sized with headroom.

options.text: It silently converts into a B-Tree
options.feedback: Incorrect: it fails insertion once max_kicks is reached.

options.text: False negatives start occurring for existing keys
options.feedback: Incorrect: existing keys remain intact; new inserts fail until resized.

learningJourney.explanation: Because multiple keys hash onto overlapping bit positions, clearing a `1` bit to `0` when deleting `key_A` can silently break `key_B`—violating the **zero false negatives** invariant. Meanwhile, **Counting Bloom Filters** replace each bit with a 4-bit counter (4x RAM overhead) and suffer counter overflow if a hot key is inserted repeatedly.

ideas.title: Cache Penetration Shield
ideas.description: Checking a filter in RAM before querying Disk/Redis rejects non-existent IDs (e.g., crawler 404 storms) in nanoseconds.

ideas.title: LSM-Tree SSTable Skip
ideas.description: RocksDB/Cassandra attach per-SSTable Bloom filters so point lookups skip 99% of disk SSTables that do not contain the key.

learningJourney.title: Where Bloom vs. Cuckoo Filters Fit Best
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: match immutable SSTables to Bloom filters and mutable blocklists/caches to Cuckoo filters.
learningJourney.explanation: Use **standard Bloom filters** for **immutable** datasets such as RocksDB/LevelDB SSTable blocks or daily batch snapshots. Use **Cuckoo filters** for **mutable** sets (session revocation lists, CDN one-hit-wonder admission caches, or active feature-flag memberships) where entries are frequently added and removed.

learningJourney.title: Sizing Bits-per-Key, Load Factor & Rebuild Thresholds
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: bound Cuckoo load factor below 95% and guard against insertion failure.
learningJourney.explanation: Size Bloom filters with explicit `(n, p)` budgets (`~10 bits/key` for `1%` FP, `~14.4 bits/key` for `0.1%` FP). For Cuckoo filters, cap occupancy at **90–95%** (`bucket_size = 4`) and bound eviction loops (`max_kicks = 500`); if an insert exhausts `max_kicks`, trigger an asynchronous double-capacity rebuild.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
import math

def bloom_sizing(expected_items: int, fp_rate: float) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (num_bits, num_hashes) for target expected_items and false-positive rate."""
    if expected_items <= 0 or not (0 < fp_rate < 1):
        raise ValueError("expected_items must be > 0 and 0 < fp_rate < 1")
    m = int(math.ceil(-(expected_items * math.log(fp_rate)) / (math.log(2) ** 2)))
    k = max(1, int(round((m / expected_items) * math.log(2))))
    return m, k
```

learningJourney.title: Bloom vs. Counting Bloom vs. Cuckoo vs. Ribbon Filters
learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare RAM per key, cache misses, deletion support, and static vs. dynamic workloads.
learningJourney.explanation: RocksDB's newer **Ribbon Filters** save ~30% RAM over Bloom filters for static immutable SSTables, while **Cuckoo Filters** win for dynamic sets needing deletion and 2-bucket cache locality.

benefits: Simple, zero resize failures, ~9.6 bits/key at 1% FP.
costs: No deletion; k=7 random bit probes cause k CPU cache misses.

benefits: Supports deletion; only 2 cache-line lookups; smaller than Bloom at <3% FP.
costs: Inserts fail above ~95% occupancy; must not delete keys that were never inserted.

learningJourney.title: Two-Stage CDN One-Hit-Wonder Filter + LSM SSTable Point Lookups
learningJourney.purpose: Production architecture: combine rotating Cuckoo filters with SSD caches to cut write amplification.
learningJourney.explanation: CDNs use a **rotating Cuckoo/Bloom admission filter** in RAM: an object is only written to NVMe SSD on its *second* request, cutting SSD write wear by 40–60% from one-hit-wonder tails while expiring old entries cleanly via filter rotation.

relationships.description: Connects Blue-Green Deployment to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Maintaining two parallel production environments behind an L7 router for atomic cutovers and sub-5-second rollbacks.
concepts.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of blue-green deployments—from L7 target-group swaps and expand-and-contract schemas to connection-pool sizing and Kafka consumer coordination.

spark.summary: Blue-green deployment maintains two identical production environments—one active (Blue) and one idle or staging (Green)—and shifts 100% of live traffic at the load balancer or DNS layer once Green passes smoke tests, enabling sub-second rollback by reversing the router pointer.

spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Blue-green deployment** decouples **deployment** (provisioning new compute, pulling containers, running additive migrations, verifying health) from **release** (exposing live user traffic).

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Blue-Green Provision -> Bake -> Atomic Flip / Rollback State Machine (BLUE LIVE (100%) -> GREEN BAKE (100%) -> INSTANT ROLLBACK); Expand Migration -> Green Smoke Test -> ALB Target Swap -> Drain (CD Pipeline -> Postgres (Expand) -> L7 ALB / Envoy -> Green (v2.15)); L7 ALB Swap -> Blue/Green Fleets -> PgBouncer -> Expand-Only Postgres (L7 ALB / Envoy -> Green (Active) -> Blue (Standby) -> PgBouncer + PG).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare compute overhead, rollback speed, and blast radius across the three standard deployment strategies. Production blue-green setups place **PgBouncer** between the Blue/Green fleets and PostgreSQL so doubling application pods never exhausts DB connections, while **AWS ALB / Envoy**.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore expand-and-contract DB migrations, graceful shutdowns, and canary rollbacks.

learningJourney.title: What is Blue-Green Deployment
learningJourney.explanation:
**Blue-green deployment** decouples **deployment** (provisioning new compute, pulling containers, running additive migrations, verifying health) from **release** (exposing live user traffic). Two parallel environments—**Blue** (currently live) and **Green** (newly provisioned)—sit behind a single L7 routing control plane (AWS ALB target groups, Envoy/Istio `VirtualService`, or Kubernetes `Service` selector).

Until Green passes automated smoke and synthetic checks on an isolated test listener, zero external users touch it. Release is an atomic pointer flip (`100% Blue -> 100% Green`), and rollback flips the pointer back in under 5 seconds.

sectionDiagram.summary: Keeping Blue warm during the bake window enables sub-5-second rollback via an L7 router swap.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Expand-and-Contract & L7 Swaps (and why DNS/destructive DDL fail)
learningJourney.explanation:
Blue-green fails catastrophically if you treat the database or DNS naively:

1. **Backward-Incompatible Schema**: Dropping a column, renaming a field, or changing a Redis JSON/Kafka Avro format breaks Blue the moment you roll back. Always use **Expand-and-Contract** (additive nullable column first; drop old column only *after* bake).
2. **DNS TTL Caching**: Route 53 weighted DNS fails for instant swaps because recursive resolvers and JVM `networkaddress.cache.ttl` ignore low TTLs.
3. **DB Connection Pool Exhaustion**: During the 30-minute bake, *both* Blue and Green hold open pools against PostgreSQL—doubling `max_connections` demand.

learningJourney.title: Where Blue-Green fits (and when Canary wins)
learningJourney.explanation: Blue-green shines when you want **zero version skew** (only one version serves production at a time) and **instant rollback**, provided you can afford 2x compute during cutover.

comparison.choice: Stateless APIs & Monoliths Requiring Zero Version Skew
benefits: No mixed v1/v2 responses for a single user session; instant <5s rollback.
costs: Requires 200% peak compute and 2x DB connection capacity during the bake window.

benefits: Validates a brand-new OS/K8s node group under synthetic load before flipping traffic.
costs: Slow provisioning for huge stateful fleets.

comparison.choice: Avoid: High-Risk Changes Without Blast-Radius Limits
benefits: Use Canary (1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%) when a bug could impact 100% of users on flip.
costs: Blue-green's 0% -> 100% flip exposes all users immediately if smoke tests miss a production edge case.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Blue-Green Routing, Draining, and Schemas are managed
learningJourney.explanation:
Enforce four operational guardrails:

1. **L7 Selector / Target Group Flip**: Switch traffic inside the VPC via Kubernetes `Service` selectors, Envoy `VirtualService`, or AWS ALB listener rules.
2. **Expand-and-Contract DDL**: Ship additive migrations in PR 1, deploy Green in PR 2, contract old columns only after bake.
3. **PgBouncer / Pool Sizing**: Route both colors through PgBouncer so 2x app pools don't exhaust Postgres `max_connections`.
4. **Pre-Warming Caches**: Replay read-only shadow traffic or warm local caches on Green before flipping live traffic.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Kubernetes Service selector flip for atomic Blue -> Green cutover
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: prod
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: orders-api
    slot: green # atomic flip from 'blue' -> 'green' (rollback flips back to 'blue')
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
# Pod graceful drain matching ALB deregistration_delay (30s)
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 35
  containers:
    - name: orders-api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec: { command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] } # wait for kube-proxy/endpoints sync
```

spark.summary: B-Trees update fixed-size disk pages (4-16 KiB) in place for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes sequentially in memory (MemTable + WAL) and merge immutable sorted runs (SSTables) in the background for orders-of-magnitude higher write throughput.

spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Storage engines bridge volatile RAM and persistent block storage (NVMe/SSD).

learningJourney.title: What are B-Trees and LSM-Trees
learningJourney.explanation:
Storage engines bridge volatile RAM and persistent block storage (NVMe/SSD). A **B+Tree** (8 KiB pages in PostgreSQL, 16 KiB in InnoDB) organizes keys in mutable, fixed-size pages linked in sorted order; with height 3–4 for 1B+ rows, internal nodes stay cached in RAM so point lookups need at most 1–2 disk reads.

A **Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)** (RocksDB, Cassandra, Pebble) never mutates on-disk blocks in place. Writes append to a sequential WAL and an in-memory skiplist (`MemTable`), flushing immutable sorted `SSTables` (~64 MiB) to disk and merging them asynchronously in the background.

sectionDiagram.title: B+Tree Mutable Page Lookup vs. LSM-Tree MemTable/SSTable Hierarchy

cards.label: B+Tree Read Path
cards.detail: Traverses 3-4 cached internal pages to a single mutable leaf page (predictable p99).

cards.label: LSM Write Path
cards.detail: Appends sequentially to WAL + MemTable; zero random page rewrites on the hot path.

cards.label: Bloom Filter Guard
cards.detail: 10 bits/key (~1% FP) lets LSM point reads skip SSTables that do not contain the key.

sectionDiagram.summary: B+Trees pay random-write amplification for 1-lookup reads; LSM-Trees batch sequential writes and pay background compaction.

learningJourney.title: Why we need LSM-Trees (and the RUM Conjecture trade-offs)
learningJourney.explanation:
Under heavy random-key `INSERT`/`UPDATE` workloads (time-series, IoT, write-heavy KV), B+Trees suffer **10x–30x+ write amplification** because modifying 100 bytes dirties an entire 8–16 KiB page (plus full-page WAL writes).

However, the **RUM Conjecture** proves you cannot minimize Read, Update/Write, and Memory/Space overhead simultaneously. LSM-Trees face two signature failure modes: **L0 Compaction Stalls** (hitting `level0_stop_writes_trigger`, default 36 in RocksDB, freezes all writes) and **Tombstone Scan Degradation** on range queries over deleted keys.

sectionDiagram.title: WAL + MemTable -> Immutable L0 -> Leveled Compaction

cards.label: Sequential I/O
cards.detail: Writes never seek random B-Tree leaf pages; MemTable flushes sequentially.

cards.label: Write-Stall Risk
cards.detail: If background compaction falls behind L0 flushes, RocksDB throttles or stops foreground writes.

cards.label: WiscKey / Titan
cards.detail: Separating large values (>1 KiB) into an append-only vLog cuts compaction write amplification sharply.

sectionDiagram.summary: LSM-Trees convert random writes into sequential flushes, but compaction bandwidth must keep pace with ingestion.

learningJourney.title: Where B-Trees and LSM-Trees belong
learningJourney.explanation: Match the storage engine to your read/write ratio, range-scan frequency, and latency SLA.

benefits: Predictable point & range read latency; strong in-place MVCC/row-lock semantics for OLTP.
costs: High random-write amplification (10-30x+) and page fragmentation under heavy random inserts.

benefits: High write throughput, ~10x space amplification control, fast point reads with Bloom filters.
costs: Higher compaction write amplification than Size-Tiered; L0 stalls if compaction lags.

benefits: Lowest write amplification for append-heavy time-series and logging workloads.
costs: Up to 50% temporary disk space overhead during major compactions; slower point/range reads.

learningJourney.title: How Compaction, Bloom Filters, and Checkpoints are tuned
learningJourney.explanation:
Tune each engine around its bottleneck:

1. **LSM-Tree**: Size `bits_per_key = 10` (~1% false positive Bloom filter), pin L0/L1 index & filter blocks in block cache, and dedicate enough background compaction threads (`max_background_jobs`) so `L0` never hits `level0_stop_writes_trigger`.
2. **B+Tree**: Keep working set in `shared_buffers` / `innodb_buffer_pool_size` (~70-80% RAM), set `checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9`, and use k-ordered primary keys (UUIDv7 / Snowflake) instead of random UUIDv4 to eliminate page splits.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: B+Tree vs. Leveled LSM vs. Size-Tiered LSM
learningJourney.explanation: Compare page unit, read/write amplification, and compaction behavior across the three dominant disk-backed index families.

benefits: 1-2 IOs on cold point reads; zero compaction stalls; fast ordered range scans.
costs: Random-write amplification and B-Tree page splits on random UUID keys.

benefits: Disjoint key ranges per level L1+; low space amplification (~1.1x) and good read p99.
costs: 10-30x compaction write amplification as levels merge repeatedly.

benefits: Lowest write amplification; ideal for write-once immutable time-series.
costs: High read amplification and 2x disk headroom required for major compaction.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Distributed KV Store (Multi-Raft + RocksDB + Titan)
learningJourney.explanation: Distributed NewSQL/KV engines like **TiKV** and **CockroachDB** (Pebble) run an LSM-Tree per node underneath **Multi-Raft** consensus groups. Separating large values (>1 KiB) into an append-only **Titan/vLog** keeps the LSM key-index compact in RAM while bounding compaction I/O.

options.feedback: Correct: monotonic keys append to the rightmost leaf page (staying hot in RAM), whereas random keys dirty pages across the entire tree.

options.feedback: WAL is always active; the bottleneck is random leaf-page I/O and splits.

options.text: B+Trees cannot store 128-bit values
options.feedback: B+Trees store 128-bit UUIDs natively; only key ordering affects page locality.

relationships.description: Bulkheads limit damage; breakers stop calling failing deps.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

concepts.tagline: Partitioning thread pools, connection pools, and tenant quotas into isolated compartments to bound blast radius.
concepts.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of bulkheads—from Little's Law pool sizing and semaphore vs. thread-pool bulkheads to shuffle sharding.

spark.summary: The bulkhead pattern partitions shared compute, thread pools, connection pools, and memory into isolated compartments so a slow or failing downstream dependency exhausts only its own quota rather than sinking the entire service.
spark.keyTakeaway: Timeouts and circuit breakers react after failures happen; bulkheads bound the blast radius structurally before a single slow dependency can starve unrelated endpoints.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Named after watertight compartments in a ship's hull, the **bulkhead pattern** divides finite system resources—worker threads, HikariCP DB connections, memory, or tenant shards—into bounded, independent pools.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts API Server -> Isolated Checkout & ML Ranker Bulkhead Pools (200 API Threads -> Checkout Pool (40) -> ML Ranker Pool (25) -> /healthz Pool); ML Ranker Stall: Unisolated Collapse vs. Bulkhead Fast-Fail (Clients -> Bulkhead (25) -> ML Ranker (Hung) -> Checkout Pool); Bulkhead + Circuit Breaker Admission State Machine (ADMIT -> FAST-SHED -> BREAKER OPEN).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose between in-process semaphores, isolated thread pools, and mesh-level concurrency caps. At scale, **Envoy** enforces `max_requests` and `max_pending_requests` per upstream cluster at the sidecar/gateway layer, while multi-tenant worker fleets use **shuffle sharding**.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore thread-pool priority inversion, Little's Law pool sizing, and circuit-breaker composition.

learningJourney.title: What is the Bulkhead Pattern
learningJourney.explanation:
Named after watertight compartments in a ship's hull, the **bulkhead pattern** divides finite system resources—worker threads, HikariCP DB connections, memory, or tenant shards—into bounded, independent pools.

If one downstream dependency hangs (e.g., an ML Ranker stalls at 10s socket timeouts) or one noisy tenant floods the system, only its assigned compartment fills up and sheds load. Unrelated critical endpoints (`/checkout`, `/healthz`) keep running at normal latency.

learningJourney.explanation:
Without bulkheads, a service with 200 worker threads calling a hanging dependency at 100 RPS exhausts all 200 threads within **2 seconds**—even with a 2-second timeout! Every unrelated endpoint and `/healthz` probe stalls, causing Kubernetes to kill and restart healthy pods.

Watch three bulkhead anti-patterns:
1. **Queue Bloat**: Setting `queueCapacity = 500` turns fast-fail into a 500-request latency trap where callers time out in the queue.
2. **Shared Hidden Bottlenecks**: Isolating HTTP threads while sharing *one* HikariCP pool, *one* DNS resolver (`systemd-resolved`), or *one* NAT ephemeral port table still allows cascading collapse.
3. **Retry Amplification**: Retrying rejected bulkhead calls without jitter multiplies load.

spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Caching** stores the result of an expensive database query, computation, or RPC in fast memory (in-process L1 or distributed Redis/Memcached) so subsequent reads reuse it in sub-millisecond time.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts App -> L1/Redis Cache -> Singleflight Guard -> PostgreSQL (API Service -> Redis (L2) -> Singleflight -> PostgreSQL); Cache-Aside Miss Coalescing & Post-Commit Invalidation (Reader 1..N -> Singleflight -> Redis -> Postgres); Postgres Commit -> Debezium CDC -> Redis DEL + L1 Pub/Sub Purge (Postgres Commit -> Debezium Relay -> Redis L2 DEL -> L1 Pub/Sub Purge).

learningJourney.title: What is Caching
learningJourney.explanation:
**Caching** stores the result of an expensive database query, computation, or RPC in fast memory (in-process L1 or distributed Redis/Memcached) so subsequent reads reuse it in sub-millisecond time.

Every cache design revolves around five core primitives: **Cache Hit** (served from cache), **Cache Miss** (computed/fetched from source of truth), **TTL** (expiry window bounding staleness), **Invalidation** (deleting/updating on write), and **Eviction** (LRU/LFU removal when RAM is full).

learningJourney.title: Why we need Stampede, Avalanche & Penetration Defenses
learningJourney.explanation:
A naive cache works fine in calm traffic and collapses on bad days due to three failure modes:

1. **Cache Avalanche**: Thousands of keys loaded at deploy time share the exact same TTL (`300s`) and expire simultaneously, sending a flood of misses to PostgreSQL. *Fix*: Add random TTL jitter (`300s +/- 30s`).
2. **Hot-Key Stampede (Breakdown)**: One viral key (`product:42`) expires while 5,000 RPS hit it—all 5,000 threads miss and hammer the DB at once. *Fix*: Request coalescing (`singleflight`) or probabilistic early refresh.
3. **Cache Penetration**: Attackers query nonexistent IDs (`product:-999`), bypassing the cache every time. *Fix*: Bloom filters or short-TTL negative caching (`NULL` sentinel).

```python
# Cache-aside with random TTL jitter, negative caching, and per-key coalescing (Python)
import random, threading

_inflight_locks: dict[str, threading.Lock] = {}
_registry_lock = threading.Lock()

def get_product_cached(redis, db, product_id: int, base_ttl: int = 300):
    key = f"product:{product_id}"
    cached = redis.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return None if cached == b"__NULL__" else cached

    with _registry_lock:
        key_lock = _inflight_locks.setdefault(key, threading.Lock())

    with key_lock: # single-process stampede guard
        cached = redis.get(key)
        if cached is not None:
            return None if cached == b"__NULL__" else cached
        row = db.fetch_product(product_id)
        jittered_ttl = base_ttl + random.randint(-30, 30) # avalanche guard
        if row is None:
            redis.setex(key, 60, b"__NULL__") # negative cache stops penetration
            return None
        redis.setex(key, jittered_ttl, row)
        return row
```

knowledgeCheck.question: Every night at 00:00 UTC, 50,000 cached product keys expire at the exact same second and PostgreSQL CPU spikes to 100%. What is this failure mode and its fix?

options.text: Cache Avalanche; add random TTL jitter (e.g., base_ttl + random(-30s, +30s)) to spread expirations
options.feedback: Correct: simultaneous expiration of many keys is a cache avalanche; random TTL jitter staggers refills smoothly.

options.text: Cache Penetration; add a Bloom filter
options.feedback: Penetration is caused by repeated queries for nonexistent keys, not synchronized TTL expiry.

options.text: Hot-Key Stampede; increase Redis maxmemory
options.feedback: Increasing maxmemory does not stop TTL expirations from firing simultaneously.

options.text: Using Write-Behind (Write-Back) eliminates all latency and consistency trade-offs
options.feedback: Incorrect: every production option in Distributed & Application Caching carries concrete latency, consistency, or operational costs.

options.text: Advantage: Only caches actually requested keys; resilient if Redis is flushed or restarts. Cost: First read is slow (miss penalty); invalidation and refill can race under concurrent writes.
options.feedback: Correct: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) delivers only caches actually requested keys; resilient if Redis is flushed or restarts. while requiring you to manage first read is slow (miss penalty); invalidation and refill can race under concurrent writes.

options.text: Advantage: Cache stays warm on writes; consistent read-after-write through the cache tier. It has zero operational or latency overhead compared to Write-Through.
options.feedback: Not quite: that describes Write-Through, whereas Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) specifically trades off: First read is slow (miss penalty); invalidation and refill can race under concurrent writes.

learningJourney.title: What is Caching
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Caching works from first principles.
learningJourney.explanation:
**Caching** stores the result of an expensive database query, computation, or RPC in fast memory (in-process L1 or distributed Redis/Memcached) so subsequent reads reuse it in sub-millisecond time.

Every cache design revolves around five core primitives: **Cache Hit** (served from cache), **Cache Miss** (computed/fetched from source of truth), **TTL** (expiry window bounding staleness), **Invalidation** (deleting/updating on write), and **Eviction** (LRU/LFU removal when RAM is full).

sectionDiagram.title: App -> L1/Redis Cache -> Singleflight Guard -> PostgreSQL

cards.label: Cache-Aside Read
cards.detail: On hit, return in <1 ms; on miss, coalesce via singleflight, query Postgres, and SETEX with jitter.

cards.label: Delete-on-Write
cards.detail: After committing a DB update, DEL product:42 rather than trying to race-update the cached JSON.

cards.label: Eviction Budget
cards.detail: Configure maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru/lfu so Redis never OOMs under burst.

sectionDiagram.summary: Keeping PostgreSQL as the clear source of truth with TTL jitter and singleflight prevents both staleness and meltdowns.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Stampede, Avalanche & Penetration Defenses
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Stampede, Avalanche & Penetration Defenses under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
A naive cache works fine in calm traffic and collapses on bad days due to three failure modes:

1. **Cache Avalanche**: Thousands of keys loaded at deploy time share the exact same TTL (`300s`) and expire simultaneously, sending a flood of misses to PostgreSQL. *Fix*: Add random TTL jitter (`300s +/- 30s`).
2. **Hot-Key Stampede (Breakdown)**: One viral key (`product:42`) expires while 5,000 RPS hit it—all 5,000 threads miss and hammer the DB at once. *Fix*: Request coalescing (`singleflight`) or probabilistic early refresh.
3. **Cache Penetration**: Attackers query nonexistent IDs (`product:-999`), bypassing the cache every time. *Fix*: Bloom filters or short-TTL negative caching (`NULL` sentinel).

learningJourney.title: What is a Canary Deployment
learningJourney.explanation:
**Canary deployment** treats a production rollout as a **controlled experiment**. Instead of flipping 100% of users at once, you deploy the new version (`v4.2`) alongside the live baseline (`v4.1`), shift a tiny L7 traffic slice (e.g., `2%`) via Istio `VirtualService`, AWS ALB weighted target groups, or NGINX Ingress, and run **Automated Canary Analysis (ACA)**.

Tools like **Argo Rollouts + Kayenta** compare canary vs. baseline on `http_5xx`, `p99` latency, and saturation using non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U), promoting `2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%` or aborting to `0%` in under 10 seconds.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Statistical Canary Analysis (and naive canary traps)
learningJourney.explanation:
Four common mistakes turn canary deployments into false confidence or noisy rollbacks:

1. **Pod-Ratio Splitting**: Without an L7 proxy, 1 canary pod out of 4 total pods forces a **25% minimum blast radius**, not 1%.
2. **Underpowered Sample Size**: Detecting a 0.2% -> 1.0% error jump (95% confidence, 80% power) needs ~1,500–2,000 requests per cohort. At 500 RPM, a 1% canary (5 RPM) takes 5+ hours to reach significance!
3. **NAT IP Sticky Skew**: Hashing on client IP behind a corporate NAT routes 20% of enterprise traffic into a '1%' canary—hash on `user_id` or `session_id`.
4. **Baseline Cold-Start Drift**: Comparing a cold canary pod against a warm 20-pod baseline with full JIT/L1 caches triggers false p99 alarms.

benefits: Reaches 2,000+ canary samples in minutes at 1–5% weight; fast statistical confidence.

costs: Teams must clean up stale feature flags regularly to avoid dead code paths.

benefits: Use Blue-Green + synthetic smoke tests or shadow reads instead of waiting hours for 1% significance.
costs: 1% of 50 RPM is 0.5 RPM—random noise dominates statistical tests.

learningJourney.title: How Argo Rollouts, Weights, and PromQL Gates are configured
learningJourney.explanation: Define explicit step weights, pause windows, and PromQL abort thresholds covering availability (`http_5xx`), tail latency (`p99`), and saturation (CPU/heap).
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Argo Rollouts Canary strategy with Istio L7 split & Prometheus AnalysisTemplate
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: payments-authorizer
spec:
  replicas: 20
  strategy:
    canary:
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService: { name: payments-vsvc, routes: [primary] }
      steps:
        - setWeight: 2
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - analysis:
            templates: [{ templateName: canary-golden-signals }]
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
```

learningJourney.title: What are CAP and PACELC
learningJourney.explanation:
Eric Brewer's **CAP Theorem** (Gilbert & Lynch, 2002) proves that when a network partition (**P**) splits a distributed store, it must choose between:
- **Consistency (C — Linearizability)**: Every read returns the most recent completed write in real-time order (or an error).
- **Availability (A)**: Every non-failing node returns a non-error response, even if stale.

**PACELC** (Daniel Abadi, 2012) adds the missing half: **if P** (partition), choose **A or C**; **else (E)** (normal operation), choose **L (latency) or C (consistency)**.

cards.label: PC/EC (etcd, Spanner)
cards.detail: Majority (N1+N2) commits $80; isolated N3 rejects writes/reads to preserve linearizability.

cards.label: PA/EL (Dynamo, Cassandra)
cards.detail: Isolated N3 still accepts writes locally, risking divergent values reconciled later via CRDTs/LWW.

cards.label: Normal-Op Latency Tax
cards.detail: Even without a partition, PC/EC pays cross-node RTT on writes while PA/EL responds locally.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Consistency Models (and how naive assumptions fail)
learningJourney.explanation:
Treating 'CP vs AP' as a binary switch leads to three expensive production failures:

1. **Quorum Without Linearizability**: Setting $W + R > N$ (e.g., $N=3, W=2, R=2$) ensures overlap in Dynamo-style stores, *but* without leader/read-repair coordination, concurrent writes + partial propagation can still violate linearizability.
2. **Clock-Skew LWW Overwrites**: Using Last-Write-Wins (LWW) with wall clocks when NTP drifts 150 ms lets older writes silently overwrite newer writes.
3. **Asymmetric / Gray Partitions**: N1 can reach N2, N2 can reach N3, but N1 cannot reach N3—breaking naive health checks.

sectionDiagram.summary: Reading from async replicas violates read-your-own-writes; linearizable reads require quorum ReadIndex or valid leader leases.

ideas.description: Linearizability (strongest, real-time) > Sequential > Causal (preserves happens-before) > Eventual (converges if writes stop).

learningJourney.title: How Quorums, Session Consistency, and Conflict Resolution are managed
learningJourney.explanation:
Bridge consistency and latency in application code:

1. **Read-Your-Own-Writes**: Pin a user's reads to the primary (or pass a monotonic LSN/commit token) for a few seconds after their write.
2. **Never Use Wall-Clock LWW for Critical State**: Use CRDTs (OR-Set, PN-Counter) or HLC/version vectors instead of raw timestamps.
3. **Leader Leases / ReadIndex**: In Raft stores, serve linearizable reads via `ReadIndex` without writing a log entry.

learningJourney.title: What are CAP and PACELC
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how CAP and PACELC works from first principles.
learningJourney.explanation:
Eric Brewer's **CAP Theorem** (Gilbert & Lynch, 2002) proves that when a network partition (**P**) splits a distributed store, it must choose between:
- **Consistency (C — Linearizability)**: Every read returns the most recent completed write in real-time order (or an error).
- **Availability (A)**: Every non-failing node returns a non-error response, even if stale.

**PACELC** (Daniel Abadi, 2012) adds the missing half: **if P** (partition), choose **A or C**; **else (E)** (normal operation), choose **L (latency) or C (consistency)**.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Consistency Models (and how naive assumptions fail)
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Consistency Models under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
Treating 'CP vs AP' as a binary switch leads to three expensive production failures:

1. **Quorum Without Linearizability**: Setting $W + R > N$ (e.g., $N=3, W=2, R=2$) ensures overlap in Dynamo-style stores, *but* without leader/read-repair coordination, concurrent writes + partial propagation can still violate linearizability.
2. **Clock-Skew LWW Overwrites**: Using Last-Write-Wins (LWW) with wall clocks when NTP drifts 150 ms lets older writes silently overwrite newer writes.
3. **Asymmetric / Gray Partitions**: N1 can reach N2, N2 can reach N3, but N1 cannot reach N3—breaking naive health checks.

learningJourney.title: What is Capacity Planning & Forecasting
learningJourney.explanation:
**Capacity planning** ensures every tier—compute, RAM, storage IOPS, network bandwidth, and third-party quotas—can absorb both organic demand and sudden failover shifts within latency SLOs.

Two quantitative laws anchor the math:
1. **Little's Law ($L = \lambda \cdot W$)**: Average concurrency $L$ equals arrival rate $\lambda$ (RPS) times response time $W$ (sec). If DB lock contention doubles $W$ from `50 ms` to `100 ms`, required threads/pods $L$ double immediately at constant RPS!
2. **Universal Scalability Law (USL)**: $C(N) = \frac{N}{1 + \alpha(N - 1) + \beta N(N - 1)}$ models both **contention** ($\alpha$, lock/queue waits) and **coherency delay** ($\beta$, cache invalidation), showing where adding nodes actually *reduces* throughput.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Saturation Curves (and why average CPU lies)
learningJourney.explanation:
Sizing from `40% average CPU` fails during real spikes for three reasons:

1. **Coordinated Omission in Load Tests**: Naive load generators pause when the server slows down, hiding the p99 latency cliff until real users hit it.
2. **Cold-Cache Thundering Herd**: Pre-scaling stateless pods without warming Redis or CDN sends 100% of peak traffic straight to PostgreSQL.
3. **Ephemeral Port & Conntrack Exhaustion**: High-RPS services without HTTP keep-alive exhaust Linux `ip_local_port_range` or `nf_conntrack_max` long before CPU hits 50%.

learningJourney.title: How Little's Law & N-1 Failover Budgets are calculated
learningJourney.explanation: Build a repeatable capacity spreadsheet or script that computes required pods, DB connections, and N-1 zone headroom from target RPS and load-tested p95 latency.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
# Little's Law + N-1 AZ Failover Capacity Calculator (Python)
import math

def size_service_fleet(
    peak_rps: float,
    target_latency_s: float,
    concurrency_per_pod: int,
    az_count: int = 3,
    max_util: float = 0.70,
) -> dict:
    # Little's Law: L = lambda * W
    required_concurrency = peak_rps * target_latency_s
    active_pods_needed = math.ceil(required_concurrency / (concurrency_per_pod * max_util))
    # N-1 AZ survival: remaining (az_count - 1) zones must carry 100% of active_pods_needed
    pods_per_az = math.ceil(active_pods_needed / (az_count - 1))
    total_pods = pods_per_az * az_count
    return {
        "littles_law_concurrency": round(required_concurrency, 1),
        "min_pods_steady": active_pods_needed,
        "total_pods_n_minus_1": total_pods,
    }
```

learningJourney.title: What is CDN Edge Caching
learningJourney.explanation:
A **Content Delivery Network (CDN)** is a globally distributed reverse-proxy tier that terminates TCP/QUIC and TLS at Points of Presence (PoPs) 5–20 ms from end users.

Using **BGP Anycast**, every PoP announces the same IP prefix so routers send each user to the topologically closest healthy PoP. Inside HTTP headers, `max-age` controls the **browser** cache while `s-maxage` controls the **shared CDN** cache—letting you cache aggressively at the edge (e.g., 24h) with instant surrogate-key purging while keeping browser TTLs short (60s).

learningJourney.title: Why we need Key Normalization & Collapse Controls (and cache-busting traps)
learningJourney.explanation:
Misconfigured CDNs silently drop from 99% hit rate to 0% and DDoS your own origin:

1. **Query-String Cache Busting**: Marketing links append unique `?fbclid=xyz` or `?utm_source=ig` parameters, creating millions of distinct cache keys for the exact same page.
2. **Cookie Poisoning**: An analytics script sets a session cookie on the root domain, and default CDN rules bypass caching whenever a `Cookie` header is present.
3. **Vary-Header Explosion**: Returning `Vary: User-Agent` fragments the cache across thousands of browser strings instead of normalizing to `mobile`/`desktop`.

concepts.name: Change Data Capture (CDC)

relationships.description: Connects Change Data Capture (CDC) to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Streaming committed row-level mutations from database WAL/binlogs into Kafka without dual-write races or polling load.
concepts.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of CDC—from pgoutput WAL decoding and initial snapshots to the Transactional Outbox pattern and replication-slot safety.

spark.summary: Change Data Capture (CDC) streams row-level inserts, updates, and deletes directly from a database's transaction log (WAL/binlog/oplog) into event buses like Kafka—eliminating dual-write race conditions and heavy polling queries.
spark.keyTakeaway: Stop dual-writing to your database and Kafka in application code: tail the committed transaction log (e.g., Debezium + PostgreSQL pgoutput) and pair it with the Transactional Outbox pattern for clean domain events.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Change Data Capture (CDC)** converts a database's internal **Write-Ahead Log (WAL)** or **binlog** into an append-only stream of committed row-level mutations (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`).

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts PostgreSQL pg_wal (pgoutput) -> Debezium -> Kafka -> Search / OLAP (Order Service Tx -> pg_wal (pgoutput) -> Debezium Connect -> OpenSearch / Iceberg); Single ACID Commit -> Debezium Outbox Router -> Ordered Domain Event (Order Service -> Postgres + Outbox -> Debezium -> Kafka / Consumer); Debezium Replication Slot Safety State Machine (STREAMING -> SLOT LAGGING -> SLOT DROPPED).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare primary-database overhead, delete capture, and operational complexity. Production pipelines run Debezium with the **`ExtractNewRecordState` / `EventRouter` SMT**, routing `outbox_events` directly to domain topics (`orders.events`) keyed by.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore reliable Debezium pipelines, transactional outboxes, and eliminating DB/search drift.

learningJourney.title: What is Change Data Capture (CDC)
learningJourney.explanation:
**Change Data Capture (CDC)** converts a database's internal **Write-Ahead Log (WAL)** or **binlog** into an append-only stream of committed row-level mutations (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`).

Because every ACID database already writes committed changes sequentially to its transaction log, log-based CDC (Debezium, Maxwell) attaches a lightweight reader (`pgoutput` logical replication in PostgreSQL) with ~1–3% CPU overhead. Consistent `REPEATABLE READ` **initial snapshots** bootstrap terabytes of existing rows and transition seamlessly to the exact WAL LSN.

sectionDiagram.title: PostgreSQL pg_wal (pgoutput) -> Debezium -> Kafka -> Search / OLAP

cards.label: Zero Dual-Write
cards.detail: Application writes only to Postgres; CDC never sees uncommitted or rolled-back transactions.

cards.label: Per-Key Ordering
cards.detail: Partitioning Kafka by aggregate_id preserves strict mutation order per entity.

cards.label: At-Least-Once + Idempotency
cards.detail: Consumers deduplicate replays using the monotonic WAL LSN or event version.

sectionDiagram.summary: Tailing the committed WAL guarantees DB and event-bus state never diverge.

learningJourney.title: Why we need CDC + Outbox (and why dual-writes & naive CDC fail)
learningJourney.explanation:
Writing to PostgreSQL and then calling `kafka.send()` in app code creates **dual-write drift**: if the process crashes or Kafka times out after `COMMIT`, the event is lost forever; if `kafka.send()` runs before `COMMIT` and the DB rolls back, downstream sees phantom orders.

Even with CDC, watch three operational traps:
1. **Replication Slot Disk Exhaustion**: A stopped Debezium connector holds back PostgreSQL `restart_lsn`, filling `pg_wal` until the DB crashes with `No space left on device`.
2. **Cross-Table Ordering Races**: Streaming raw `orders` and `order_items` to separate Kafka topics lets consumers see `OrderItemCreated` before `OrderCreated`—use the **Transactional Outbox** pattern!
3. **Polling `SELECT` Gaps**: Query-based polling (`WHERE updated_at > ?`) misses hard `DELETE`s and burdens the primary DB.

learningJourney.title: How Replication Slots, Outbox Cleanup, and Idempotency are managed
learningJourney.explanation:
Protect your primary database and downstream sinks:

1. **Cap Slot Retention**: Set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` (PostgreSQL 13+) so a dead CDC connector drops its slot before crashing the primary disk.
2. **Outbox Table Hygiene**: Partition `outbox` by day and `DROP` old partitions (or delete immediately in CDC if using log-only retention) to avoid vacuum bloat.
3. **Consumer Deduplication**: Track `source_lsn` or `event_id` in downstream sinks so at-least-once replays are idempotent.

learningJourney.title: What is Chaos Engineering
learningJourney.explanation:
**Chaos engineering** is empirical verification for distributed systems. Rather than *assuming* timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and multi-AZ failovers will work during an outage, you **prove** they work by injecting controlled turbulence.

Grounded in the scientific method, every experiment follows four steps: (1) define a measurable **steady state** (e.g., Checkout `success >= 99.9%`, `p99 <= 250 ms`), (2) formulate a **hypothesis**, (3) inject a **bounded fault** (e.g., 800 ms `tc netem` delay on 10% of Inventory pods), and (4) verify steady state holds or **abort automatically** if error budgets burn.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Gray-Failure Injection (and why PodChaos isn't enough)
learningJourney.explanation:
Most teams start by killing pods (`PodChaos`), which only tests clean crash-stop behavior where Kubernetes removes the pod IP immediately. Real outages are **gray failures**: `300–1,000 ms` asymmetric packet delay, `5%` packet loss, clock skew, or Redis evictions that keep TCP sockets open just long enough to exhaust thread pools.

Watch three chaos anti-patterns:
1. **Unbounded Blast Radius**: Targeting an entire namespace instead of a 5% canary or synthetic header slice.
2. **Orphaned Kernel Faults**: A crashed chaos agent leaves `tc netem` or `iptables` rules active after the experiment.
3. **Telemetry Starvation**: Injecting 100% network loss on a node cuts off Prometheus scraping, blinding your abort detector.

learningJourney.explanation: Use declarative, time-bounded CRDs (**Chaos Mesh**, **LitmusChaos**, or **AWS Fault Injection Service**) with explicit pod percentage selectors (`mode: fixed-percent`, `value: "10"`) and automated Prometheus abort alarms.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Time-bounded Chaos Mesh NetworkChaos injecting 800ms gray latency on 10% of pods
apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata:
  name: inventory-gray-latency
  namespace: prod
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: fixed-percent
  value: "10" # strict blast radius
  selector:
    namespaces: [prod]
    labelSelectors: { app: inventory-service }
  delay:
    latency: "800ms"
    jitter: "100ms"
  duration: "5m" # auto-reverts tc netem rules even if operator pauses
```

learningJourney.title: What is Chaos Engineering
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Chaos Engineering works from first principles.
learningJourney.explanation:
**Chaos engineering** is empirical verification for distributed systems. Rather than *assuming* timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and multi-AZ failovers will work during an outage, you **prove** they work by injecting controlled turbulence.

Grounded in the scientific method, every experiment follows four steps: (1) define a measurable **steady state** (e.g., Checkout `success >= 99.9%`, `p99 <= 250 ms`), (2) formulate a **hypothesis**, (3) inject a **bounded fault** (e.g., 800 ms `tc netem` delay on 10% of Inventory pods), and (4) verify steady state holds or **abort automatically** if error budgets burn.

sectionDiagram.title: Chaos Experiment Lifecycle & Automated Abort State Machine
sectionDiagram.summary: Automated abort hooks and time-bounded CRDs ensure fault injection halts and cleans up kernel rules immediately on SLO breach.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Gray-Failure Injection (and why PodChaos isn't enough)
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Gray-Failure Injection under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
Most teams start by killing pods (`PodChaos`), which only tests clean crash-stop behavior where Kubernetes removes the pod IP immediately. Real outages are **gray failures**: `300–1,000 ms` asymmetric packet delay, `5%` packet loss, clock skew, or Redis evictions that keep TCP sockets open just long enough to exhaust thread pools.

Watch three chaos anti-patterns:
1. **Unbounded Blast Radius**: Targeting an entire namespace instead of a 5% canary or synthetic header slice.
2. **Orphaned Kernel Faults**: A crashed chaos agent leaves `tc netem` or `iptables` rules active after the experiment.
3. **Telemetry Starvation**: Injecting 100% network loss on a node cuts off Prometheus scraping, blinding your abort detector.

learningJourney.title: What are CI/CD Quality Gates
learningJourney.explanation:
**CI/CD quality gates** are automated, non-negotiable verification checkpoints placed along the path from `git push` to 100% production traffic. Instead of relying on manual QA sign-offs, gates encode engineering, security, and reliability standards into executable checks.

The core design principle is **tiered latency matching** (the Testing Trophy): fast deterministic checks (`gitleaks`, `semgrep` SAST, `buf breaking`, unit tests) fail bad PRs in `<3 minutes`; Pact contract tests, Testcontainers, Trivy CVE scans, and **Cosign** signing run in the merge queue (`5–10m`); and **Canary SLO gates** verify live p99 and 5xx in production.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Tiered Gates (and how flaky/slow gates fail)
learningJourney.explanation:
Badly designed CI gates hurt both reliability and velocity:

1. **Flaky Test Erosion**: A 5% flaky integration test trains developers to hit 'Re-run' blindly, masking real regressions.
2. **Slow-Gate Queue Jamming**: Putting a 35-minute E2E suite as a blocking PR check creates a 10-PR backlog and forces teams to bundle risky giant diffs.
3. **Canary Blind Spots**: Checking only HTTP `5xx` in a canary gate misses silent latency regressions (`p99` doubling) or business conversion drops.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Fast-to-slow GitHub Actions PR quality gate workflow
name: pr-quality-gates
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  fast-static-and-unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Secret & SAST Scan
        run: |
          gitleaks detect --no-git --redact
          semgrep --config p/owasp-top-ten --error
      - name: Policy-as-Code (Conftest / OPA)
        run: conftest test deploy/k8s/*.yaml -p policy/
      - name: Unit Tests & Diff Coverage
        run: pytest --cov=app --cov-fail-under=80
```

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how CI/CD Quality Gates works from first principles.
learningJourney.explanation:
**CI/CD quality gates** are automated, non-negotiable verification checkpoints placed along the path from `git push` to 100% production traffic. Instead of relying on manual QA sign-offs, gates encode engineering, security, and reliability standards into executable checks.

The core design principle is **tiered latency matching** (the Testing Trophy): fast deterministic checks (`gitleaks`, `semgrep` SAST, `buf breaking`, unit tests) fail bad PRs in `<3 minutes`; Pact contract tests, Testcontainers, Trivy CVE scans, and **Cosign** signing run in the merge queue (`5–10m`); and **Canary SLO gates** verify live p99 and 5xx in production.

learningJourney.explanation:
Badly designed CI gates hurt both reliability and velocity:

1. **Flaky Test Erosion**: A 5% flaky integration test trains developers to hit 'Re-run' blindly, masking real regressions.
2. **Slow-Gate Queue Jamming**: Putting a 35-minute E2E suite as a blocking PR check creates a 10-PR backlog and forces teams to bundle risky giant diffs.
3. **Canary Blind Spots**: Checking only HTTP `5xx` in a canary gate misses silent latency regressions (`p99` doubling) or business conversion drops.

learningJourney.title: What is a Circuit Breaker
learningJourney.explanation:
A **circuit breaker** wraps remote RPC/HTTP calls in a three-state finite state machine:
- **CLOSED**: Normal traffic passes through while recording success/failure/slow-call outcomes in a sliding window.
- **OPEN**: When failure rate (e.g., `>= 50%`) or slow-call ratio (`> 2,000 ms`) crosses threshold, calls fail *immediately* in microseconds (`CallNotPermittedException` / `503`) without touching the network.
- **HALF-OPEN**: After `waitDurationInOpenState` (e.g., `30s` + jitter), a small probe budget (`5` requests) tests recovery before closing or re-opening.

sectionDiagram.title: Circuit Breaker CLOSED -> OPEN -> HALF-OPEN State Machine
sectionDiagram.summary: Failing fast in OPEN state protects caller thread pools and gives the degraded downstream service room to recover.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how a Circuit Breaker works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Circuit Breakers (and common misconfigurations)
learningJourney.explanation:
When a Fraud Scoring gRPC service's p99 jumps from `45 ms` to `6,000 ms`, 200 Tomcat worker threads at 100 RPS saturate in 2 seconds—crashing `/healthz` too. A circuit breaker stops calling Fraud Scoring and serves a safe fallback.

Avoid three classic breaker bugs:
1. **Counting `4xx` as Failures**: Counting `400 Bad Request` or `404 Not Found` lets one buggy client trip the breaker for *every* tenant—ignore business/client errors.
2. **Half-Open Thundering Herd**: Without `permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState` (e.g., 5) and jitter on the open timer, 100 pods probe simultaneously and re-crash the recovering service.
3. **Wrong Decorator Order**: Retrying *outside* a circuit breaker wastes retries; retrying *inside* lets a single logical call burn 3x attempts before recording 1 failure.

sectionDiagram.title: Fraud gRPC Stall -> Breaker Trips OPEN -> Order API Stays Healthy
sectionDiagram.summary: Tripping OPEN drops thread hold time from 500ms-6s down to 0ms, keeping the caller's worker pool healthy.

learningJourney.title: What are CNN, RNN, and Transformer Inductive Biases
learningJourney.explanation:
Each neural architecture encodes a structural assumption (**inductive bias**) about its input:
- **CNN (Convolutional Neural Network)**: Applies shared local spatial kernels (`3x3` conv) across 2D/3D grids, giving **translation equivariance** and low parameter count.
- **RNN / LSTM**: Updates a fixed-size hidden state sequentially $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$—giving $O(1)$ per-token inference memory, but preventing parallel training across time and suffering vanishing gradients.
- **Transformer**: Computes parallel **Scaled Dot-Product Self-Attention** $\text{Softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V$ across all tokens simultaneously ($O(1)$ sequential path length), learning global dependencies without recurrence.

learningJourney.title: Why Transformers replaced RNNs (and their O(N^2) / KV-cache bottlenecks)
learningJourney.explanation:
RNNs/LSTMs stall modern GPU clusters because step $t$ cannot compute until $t-1$ finishes, and long-range gradients decay over hundreds of steps. Transformers solve both—every token attends directly to every prior token in parallel.

However, Transformers introduce two scaling bottlenecks: **$O(N^2)$ attention matrix memory** during long-context prefill (solved via **FlashAttention** IO-aware tiling) and **linearly growing KV-Cache VRAM** during autoregressive decoding (solved via **GQA** and **PagedAttention**).

learningJourney.title: How Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Causal Masking work in code
learningJourney.explanation: Divide $QK^T$ by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to keep softmax gradients out of saturation, and apply an upper-triangular `-inf` causal mask in decoders.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
# Causal Scaled Dot-Product Self-Attention (PyTorch)
import math, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def causal_self_attention(q: torch.Tensor, k: torch.Tensor, v: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # q, k, v: (batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim)
    d_k = q.size(-1)
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(d_k)
    seq_len = q.size(-2)
    causal_mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(seq_len, seq_len, device=q.device, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
    scores = scores.masked_fill(causal_mask, float("-inf"))
    attn_weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return torch.matmul(attn_weights, v)
```

learningJourney.title: What are Columnar Analytics Engines
learningJourney.explanation:
**Columnar analytics engines** invert physical storage from row-major (all fields of row 1, then row 2) to **column-major** (all values of column A together, then column B).

Because analytical queries aggregate 2–5 columns out of a 100-column table, **projection pushdown** skips 95%+ of disk I/O. Homogeneous column values then unlock **10x–20x compression** (Dictionary encoding, Run-Length Encoding, Delta/FOR before LZ4/ZSTD), while **vectorized execution** (DuckDB, ClickHouse, Velox) processes batches of 1,024–4,096 values in CPU L1 cache with SIMD instructions.

learningJourney.title: Why Row Stores choke on OLAP (and columnar failure modes)
learningJourney.explanation:
Scanning 500M rows in PostgreSQL loads all 100 columns per 8 KiB heap page and evaluates tuple visibility row-by-row.

Yet columnar engines fail fast if misused:
1. **Unbatched Single-Row Inserts**: Inserting 1 row per HTTP request creates thousands of tiny immutable parts/files, triggering `Too many parts` errors in ClickHouse or Iceberg metadata bloat.
2. **Bad `ORDER BY` Sort Key**: Putting a high-cardinality `UUID` first in the sort key destroys RLE compression and forces full-table scans for tenant/date queries.
3. **Row-Level OLTP Updates**: Updating 1 row in Parquet/ClickHouse requires rewriting immutable segments or merge-on-read tombstones.

```sql
-- ClickHouse MergeTree with optimal sort key, Bloom skipping index, and 1-min rollup MV
CREATE TABLE events_raw (
    tenant_id LowCardinality(String),
    ts DateTime64(3),
    trace_id String,
    latency_ms UInt32,
    INDEX idx_trace trace_id TYPE bloom_filter(0.01) GRANULARITY 4
) ENGINE = MergeTree()
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)
ORDER BY (tenant_id, toStartOfHour(ts), ts);

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW events_1m_mv
ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree()
ORDER BY (tenant_id, bucket_1m)
AS SELECT
    tenant_id,
    toStartOfMinute(ts) AS bucket_1m,
    quantilesState(0.95, 0.99)(latency_ms) AS lat_q
FROM events_raw GROUP BY tenant_id, bucket_1m;
```

learningJourney.title: What is Configuration vs. Secrets Separation
learningJourney.explanation:
Modern production security splits the Twelve-Factor environment into two distinct planes:
- **Configuration Plane**: Non-sensitive behavior tuning (`LOG_LEVEL`, `DB_HOST`, `HIKARI_MAX_POOL`, `STRIPE_TIMEOUT_MS`, feature flags) that is safe to commit to Git and review in PRs.
- **Secrets Plane**: Cryptographic material, DB passwords, and API keys (`STRIPE_SK`, `JWT_PRIVATE_KEY`) that grant identity or billing authority.

**Base64 is encoding, not encryption**: never commit Kubernetes `Secret` YAML or `.env` files to Git. Instead, use **Workload Identity (IRSA / GCP WI / SPIFFE)** to eliminate static secrets altogether, and **Vault / External Secrets Operator (ESO)** for any remaining credentials.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Runtime Secret Injection & Dynamic Rotation
learningJourney.explanation:
Mixing secrets into Git or static `.env` files causes irreversible leaks—even deleting a committed key in a follow-up commit leaves it in Git history forever.

Watch three operational failure modes:
1. **Startup-Only Secret Reads**: Apps that read a secret file once in `main()` fail with `401` or `28P01` when rotated in-place; support file-watch reload or dual-key grace periods.
2. **CI/CD Exfiltration**: Printing `env` in GitHub Actions or passing `$TOKEN` as a CLI flag exposes secrets in logs and `ps aux`.
3. **Unencrypted etcd**: Kubernetes `Secret` objects are base64-encoded in etcd unless KMS envelope encryption is enabled.

learningJourney.title: What is Connection Pool Tuning
learningJourney.explanation:
Opening a fresh database connection requires a TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, auth, and a PostgreSQL backend process (`20–50 ms` and `5–10 MB` RAM). **Connection pools** (HikariCP, `pgxpool`, SQLAlchemy) amortize that setup by keeping pre-authenticated sockets warm.

Crucially, **more connections = slower database**: once active queries exceed `(core_count * 2) + effective_spindles` (~32–40 on a 16-core NVMe server), context switching and lock contention crush throughput. Always budget `pod_count * maximumPoolSize` across your *maximum* HPA pod count, or place **PgBouncer (transaction mode)** in front of PostgreSQL.

cards.label: 2x Cores Formula
cards.detail: An 8-core NVMe Postgres primary hits peak throughput around ~20-32 active connections, not 500.

cards.label: Transaction Mode
cards.detail: PgBouncer assigns a server backend only for the duration of a single SQL transaction, then reuses it.

cards.label: Workload Separation
cards.detail: Route reporting queries to a separate readerPool with longer timeouts so checkout writers never starve.

learningJourney.title: Why Naive Pool Sizing & Idle Timeouts Fail in Production
learningJourney.explanation:
Three classic connection-pool failures take down production APIs:

1. **HPA Connection Explosion**: 30 pods x `maximumPoolSize=30` = 900 connections hitting RDS (`max_connections=400`), triggering `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`.
2. **Long Transactions Pinning Connections**: Calling an external HTTP API or generating a PDF *inside* a DB transaction holds the pooled connection idle for seconds, exhausting the pool.
3. **Silent NLB/NAT TCP Drops**: Cloud load balancers silently drop idle TCP flows after `350s`; without `maxLifetime < 300s` (or shorter than DB `idle_session_timeout`) and TCP keepalives, queries hang for 15 minutes on half-open sockets.

sectionDiagram.title: HikariCP maxLifetime Rotation Preventing Stale NAT Socket Hangs
sectionDiagram.summary: Setting maxLifetime strictly shorter than NAT/firewall idle timeouts prevents silent half-open TCP hangs.

ideas.title: Little's Law Sanity Check
ideas.description: At 1,000 QPS with 5 ms query time (0.005s), L = 1,000 * 0.005 = 5 average active connections; 15-20 slots handles 3x bursts.

ideas.title: PgBouncer Tx-Mode Caveat
ideas.description: Transaction mode forbids session-level SET variables, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and temp tables unless scoped to SET LOCAL.

learningJourney.title: How HikariCP & PgBouncer Parameters are tuned
learningJourney.explanation: Set `maximumPoolSize` small, `connectionTimeout` fail-fast (`2,000 ms`), `maxLifetime` shorter than NAT/DB idle limits, and `leakDetectionThreshold` in staging/prod.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Production HikariCP + PostgreSQL timeout configuration (Spring Boot / YAML)
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10          # 10 pods * 10 = 100 max conns (or fronted by PgBouncer)
      minimum-idle: 10               # fixed-size pool avoids resize spikes
      connection-timeout: 2000       # fail fast in 2s instead of hanging 30s
      max-lifetime: 240000           # 4m (< 350s AWS NLB / NAT idle timeout)
      leak-detection-threshold: 5000 # log stack trace if conn held > 5s
      data-source-properties:
        options: "-c statement_timeout=2000 -c lock_timeout=1500"
```

costs: Cannot scale horizontally with high pod counts or serverless Lambdas.

benefits: Supports session SET/temp tables while buffering bursty client connects.
costs: Still 1:1 backend-to-active-client; minimal multiplexing gain for long-lived app pools.

benefits: High multiplexing ratio; essential for serverless/high-HPA Kubernetes fleets.
costs: Requires disabling session-level state and configuring protocol-level prepared statements (PgBouncer 1.21+).

learningJourney.title: What is Connection Pool Tuning
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Connection Pool Tuning works from first principles.
learningJourney.explanation:
Opening a fresh database connection requires a TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, auth, and a PostgreSQL backend process (`20–50 ms` and `5–10 MB` RAM). **Connection pools** (HikariCP, `pgxpool`, SQLAlchemy) amortize that setup by keeping pre-authenticated sockets warm.

Crucially, **more connections = slower database**: once active queries exceed `(core_count * 2) + effective_spindles` (~32–40 on a 16-core NVMe server), context switching and lock contention crush throughput. Always budget `pod_count * maximumPoolSize` across your *maximum* HPA pod count, or place **PgBouncer (transaction mode)** in front of PostgreSQL.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Why Naive Pool Sizing & Idle Timeouts Fail in Production under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
Three classic connection-pool failures take down production APIs:

1. **HPA Connection Explosion**: 30 pods x `maximumPoolSize=30` = 900 connections hitting RDS (`max_connections=400`), triggering `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`.
2. **Long Transactions Pinning Connections**: Calling an external HTTP API or generating a PDF *inside* a DB transaction holds the pooled connection idle for seconds, exhausting the pool.
3. **Silent NLB/NAT TCP Drops**: Cloud load balancers silently drop idle TCP flows after `350s`; without `maxLifetime < 300s` (or shorter than DB `idle_session_timeout`) and TCP keepalives, queries hang for 15 minutes on half-open sockets.

concepts.name: Consistency Patterns
concepts.tagline: Choose the right distributed consistency guarantee—from strict linearizability to causal, read-your-writes, and eventual convergence—based on user invariants and latency budgets.

spark.title: Consistency Patterns
spark.summary: Choose the right distributed consistency guarantee—from strict linearizability to causal, read-your-writes, and eventual convergence—based on user invariants and latency budgets.
spark.keyTakeaway: Strongest consistency (Linearizability) costs cross-AZ/region coordination latency; client-centric guarantees like Read-Your-Writes deliver intuitive UX at a fraction of the cost.
spark.byteSummary:
Choose the right distributed consistency guarantee—from strict linearizability to causal, read-your-writes, and eventual convergence—based on user invariants and latency budgets.

Picture a user updating their shipping address, hitting Refresh, and watching their old address reappear for two seconds.

Strongest consistency (Linearizability) costs cross-AZ/region coordination latency; client-centric guarantees like Read-Your-Writes deliver intuitive UX at a fraction of the cost.

concept.whyItMatters: Picture a user updating their shipping address, hitting Refresh, and watching their old address reappear for two seconds. Nothing crashed—the write committed to the [SQL](/domains/sql) primary, while the refresh landed on an asynchronous read replica lagging 400ms behind. Choosing the right consistency pattern lets you avoid paying global [Raft/Quorum](/concept/leader-election-patterns) latency on every read while still protecting user trust via session LSN routing.
whenToUse: Linearizability for distributed locks, leader leases, and unique username/inventory claims.
Read-Your-Writes & Monotonic Reads for user profiles, comments, and settings.
Causal Consistency for threaded discussions and collaborative state.
whenNotToUse: Paying cross-region consensus latency for analytics counters or view counts where eventual consistency suffices.
keyPoints: Linearizability provides a single global real-time order: once a write completes, every subsequent read anywhere sees it or a newer value.
Causal Consistency preserves happens-before relationships (e.g., question before answer) without blocking on unrelated concurrent writes.
Read-Your-Writes ensures a user always sees their own recent mutations—achievable via sticky replica routing, session LSN tokens, or reading from primary for N seconds after a write.
Monotonic Reads guarantees time never appears to move backward across consecutive reads (pinning a user to a replica or minimum LSN).

examples.title: Session-Token Read-Your-Writes Routing
examples.scenario: A user updates their display name (committed at primary WAL `LSN = 9042`) and immediately reloads `/profile`, which hits a read replica currently at `LSN = 9038`.
examples.outcome: The client sends `X-Min-LSN: 9042` in its session cookie; the router either waits briefly for the replica to catch up to `9042` or falls back to the primary, preventing the 'disappearing edit' bug.

tradeOffs.con: Requires quorum round-trips and fails writes during minority partitions

tradeOffs.pro: Fast replica reads most of the time

failureModes.name: Replication Lag Breaking Read-Your-Writes
failureModes.description: Write hits primary, immediate refresh hits lagging replica and returns old state.
failureModes.mitigation: Route recent writers to primary for a short window or enforce `min_lsn` on replicas.

failureModes.name: Replica Hopping Breaking Monotonic Reads
failureModes.description: Request 1 hits Replica A (LSN 100); Request 2 hits lagging Replica B (LSN 92), so data disappears.
failureModes.mitigation: Pin user session to one replica or pass `last_seen_lsn`.

commonMistakes: Confusing ACID Consistency (database constraint validity) with CAP/Distributed Consistency (linearizability across replicas).
Assuming Eventual Consistency means no coordination is needed—applications still need conflict resolution (LWW, CRDTs) and idempotency.

sections.content:
## Consistency spectrum & real-world mechanisms

| Pattern | Scope | Guarantees | Typical Implementation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Linearizable | Global (data-centric) | Real-time single-copy illusion | Raft / Paxos quorum reads (`ReadIndex`) |
| Sequential | Global | Same order for all nodes, not real-time | Single-sequencer log |
| Causal | Partial order | Preserves cause-before-effect | Vector clocks / Hybrid Logical Clocks |
| Read-Your-Writes | Per-client session | User always sees own writes | Primary-pin window or `min_lsn` cookie |
| Monotonic Reads | Per-client session | Reads never go backward in time | Sticky replica or `last_seen_lsn` |
| Eventual | Global convergence | Converges when writes cease | Async replication + LWW / CRDT |

pillars.label: All Patterns
pillars.summary: Consistency patterns determine whether reads can use fast lagging replicas or must coordinate with the primary/quorum.

pillars.label: Linearizable
pillars.summary: Every read routes to the quorum leader (or ReadIndex) so stale replicas are never observed.

pillars.label: Read-Your-Writes
pillars.summary: Router compares replica LSN against the client's session min_lsn and falls back to primary only if the replica lags behind that user's write.

normal.heading: Step 1: Mutation Commits on Primary (LSN 9042)
normal.desc: User updates profile on Primary; server returns cookie `min_lsn=9042`.

normal.heading: Step 2: Replica Reaches LSN 9042
normal.desc: Replica replays WAL to 9042. Router serves the reload directly from the fast replica.

normal.heading: Step 3: Steady-State Replica Reads
normal.desc: Subsequent reads hit replicas whenever replica_lsn >= min_lsn.

fault.heading: Step 3 (LAG!): Replica Stuck at LSN 9038
fault.desc: Replica lags at 9038 < 9042. Router detects `replica_lsn < min_lsn` and routes this single read to Primary.
